5805.t: Uncertain; possibly from Pre-Greek. Potential cognates include Spanish cuesco (“stone (of fruit)”), though this is rejected by Furnee.

5800.t: Of unclear origin. Traditionally compared with Latin carīna (“ship's keel; shell of a nut”) and Sanskrit करक (karaka, “water jar; coconut (shell)”).

5809.t: Difficult to trace. The word passed to and from a number of languages (compare Latin cubus (“mass, quantity; cube”)).

5897.t: From νοέω (noéō, “to intend, to perceive, to see, to understand”) + -μα (-mă).

5818.t: From λέκος (lékos, “dish; pot; pan”) + -άνη (-ắnē, suffix for utensil names), alleged to be from Pre-Greek; however, see λάγυνος (lắgūnos, “flask”).

5880.t: From Proto-Indo-European *morwís (“ant”). Related to Old Armenian մրջիւն (mrǰiwn) and Latin formīca and perhaps Sanskrit वल्मी (valmī).

5810.t: Perhaps from a Proto-Indo-European *ḱewk- (“white”), with cognates including Sanskrit शोचति (śócati, “to shine, suffer”) and शुक्र (śukrá, “bright, white”), and possibly Old Norse Hǿnir (“god associated with swans and storks”).

5806.t: Uncertain; Beekes and Furnee take the word as the usual Pre-Greek, while others have narrowed down the language of origin to possibly Semitic or Hurrian.

5808.t: Beekes suggests a Pre-Greek origin due to the presence of variations and rejects a derivation from κυέω (kŭéō); possibly connected to Classical Syriac ܓܘܡܐ (gūmā), Jewish Babylonian Aramaic גוגמא, גגמא (“bean”).

5811.t: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *ḱewh₁- Proto-Indo-European *-yeti Proto-Indo-European *-éyeti Proto-Indo-European *ḱuh₁éyeti Ancient Greek κύω From Proto-Indo-European *ḱewh₁- (“to swell”).

5868.t: Possibly an -ός (-ós) agent noun of ὀμείχω (omeíkhō, “to urinate”), used as a vulgar expression, but this is disputed.

5817.t: From λείχω (leíkhō, “to lick”), derived with the meaning “the one who licks”, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *leyǵʰ- (“to lick”).

5895.t: From Proto-Indo-European *h₁enos (“that one”), the source of Latin nē (“truly!”), enim (“truly”).

5821.t: From a Semitic sound plural of the etymon of λίβανος (lĭ́bănos), which Beekes says derives from a Semitic root cognate to Hebrew לָבָן (“white”) and Arabic لَبَن (laban, “milk”).

5812.t: According to Beekes, probably of Pre-Greek origin. The term has been compared to Georgian [script needed] (kotoxi, “cup”) and Mingrelian [script needed] (koto, “cup”).

5802.t: From Proto-Hellenic *kʰénkʰros, mostly derived from Proto-Indo-European *gʰer-gʰ-r-o- (“pulverized”), reduplicated from the root *gʰer- (“to rub, grind”) with dissimilation r…r > n…r, and further connected with Ancient Greek χερμάς (khermás), χεράς…

5831.t: Probably of onomatopoeic origin but compare Armenian լոր (lor, “quail”).

5872.t: The connection with Old Armenian մխեմ (mxem, “to insert; to immerse”) is obsolete and semantically doubtful.

5852.t: μερίζω (merízō, “to divide”) + -μός (-mós, event or process noun suffix)

5888.t: From Proto-Indo-European *new- (“to nod”). Cognate with Latin nutō (“to nod”), Sanskrit नव॑ते (návate).

5859.t: According to Beekes, from a noun, perhaps *μεῖρος (*meîros), which would agree with Sanskrit मर्य॑ (márya, “young man; suitor; lover”) and Avestan 𐬨𐬀𐬌𐬭𐬌𐬌𐬀 (maⁱriia, “yeoman”), or *μεῖρα (*meîră).

5830.t: An onomatopoeic word. In other Indo-European languages we find Albanian lap (“to slurp”), Proto-Slavic *lopati (“to eat greedily”), Lithuanian lapènti (“to absorb greedily”), Old English lapian (“to lap”).

5877.t: Univerbation of μή (mḗ, “so that...not, lest”) + τις (tis, “anyone”).
